h1: The 8 Best Rice Cookers Under $100 in 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best Rice Cookers Under $100: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 8 rice cookers under $100, scored on cooking logic, capacity, keep-warm, pot coating and extras like steaming and slow cook.
summary: The Cosori 10-cup fuzzy logic cooker is the best rice cooker under $100 for anyone who cooks rice several times a week, with 18 programs, a delay timer and a ceramic-coated pot. The Aroma 20-cup digital model is the best for big families, the Aroma 4/8-cup digital is the best mid-size choice, and the Elite Gourmet is the bare-minimum starter.
intro: A $100 ceiling invites a question most rice cooker guides skip: is the extra $50 over a basic cooker worth it? A one-switch pot cooks decent white rice. What a more expensive model adds is control, with programs for brown rice and grains, a timer that has dinner ready when you walk in, and a 24-hour warm setting that does not dry the bottom layer into crust.

We ranked eight cookers on that question, from a single-button Elite Gourmet to the Cosori with fuzzy logic. We reviewed spec sheets, capacity claims and accessory lists, not the cooked rice itself. Only one pick here sits in the $50 to $100 bracket, so most of this list is about how much you really need to spend, and where the cheaper Aroma and BLACK+DECKER models quietly do the job.

products.name: Cosori Rice Cooker 10 Cup, Fuzzy Logic, Ceramic Coating Inner Pot,18-in-1
products.verdict: Fuzzy logic, 18 programs, a 24-hour delay timer and a ceramic-coated pot: the only true upgrade here.
products.description:
The Cosori is the one cooker in this ranking that adjusts the cook rather than just timing it. Its fuzzy logic runs a seven-step programme, and the 18 functions cover white and brown rice with texture choices, three grains, three oat types, steamed vegetables, slow cooking and sauteing. It offers a 24-hour delay timer, 24-hour keep warm and a 1000W quick rice mode. The body is about 12.3 by 9.2 by 10.6 inches, and it costs between $50 and $100.

It wins because texture control is the real upgrade. Rinsed jasmine, sushi rice and brown rice need different cooks, and the Cosori treats them separately. The ceramic-coated pot and steamer basket are dishwasher safe, so cleanup is easy. It beats the Aroma 20-cup on programme depth but loses on raw capacity and on slow cook size.

Buy it if rice is a weekly staple. The caveat is that this is the priciest cooker in the group, and it sits near the top of the $100 budget, so if you cook rice twice a month, the Aroma digital covers you for less.
products.idealFor: Households that cook rice and grains several times a week.
products.skipIf: You eat rice rarely and want the lowest price.

products.name: Aroma Housewares 20 Cup Cooked (10 cup uncooked) Digital Rice Cooker, Slow Cooker, Food Steamer
products.verdict: Digital presets and a slow cook mode in a stainless-steel body that yields up to 20 cups cooked.
products.description:
This Aroma handles from 4 to 20 cups of cooked rice or grains, with digital presets for white rice, brown rice, steam, flash rice and slow cook. Its Sensor Logic system monitors the internal temperature through the cycle, an automatic warm setting follows every cook, and the steam tray lets you cook vegetables or fish above the rice. A measuring cup, spatula and tray come in the box. It sits in the $30 to $50 bracket.

Second place reflects scale. Almost nobody else in this price range offers a 10-cup uncooked capacity with real presets, and the slow cook setting turns it into a soup pot. It loses to the Cosori on texture programmes and pot coating, since the listing does not describe a ceramic finish.

Choose it for large families, potlucks and meal prep. Skip it if you cook for one or two, because a big pot makes small batches uneven and takes a lot of cupboard space.

products.name: AROMA Digital Rice Cooker, 4-Cup (Uncooked) / 8-Cup (Cooked), Steamer, Grain Cooker, Multicooker, 2 Qt
products.verdict: The same digital controls as the 20-cup, scaled to a family of three or four.
products.description:
This 2-quart model makes 2 to 8 cups of cooked rice, with digital controls, presets for white, brown, steam and flash rice, an automatic keep warm and Sensor Logic temperature control. A steam tray is included. It measures roughly 9.3 by 8.5 by 8.6 inches and costs $30 to $50.

It ranks third because it keeps nearly everything that makes the 20-cup good and fits a normal kitchen. The listing reminds owners that the measuring cup supplied is the only one to use, a sensible warning because it is a smaller scoop than a standard kitchen cup. It trails the 20-cup in capacity and has no slow cook mode.

It is the best choice for a household of two to four that wants presets without the Cosori's price. Rice quality will depend on following the cup rule.
pros: Digital presets at a low price
products.idealFor: Households of two to four who want presets.
products.skipIf: You want slow cooking or the largest capacity.

products.name: BLACK+DECKER 16-Cup Rice Cooker, RC516, 8-Cup Uncooked Rice, Steaming Basket
products.verdict: A no-frills 8-cup cooker with a steaming basket, glass lid and auto keep warm for under $30.
products.description:
The RC516 cooks up to 8 cups of uncooked rice, which is 16 cups cooked, using the included measuring cup. It has a removable nonstick bowl that is dishwasher safe, a tempered glass lid with a hanger, a steaming basket, a measuring cup and spoon, and two heat settings: cook, then automatic warm once the moisture is absorbed. The body is about 11.5 inches in each direction.

It takes fourth place because it matches the large Aroma on capacity at a lower price, with a simple mechanical approach. The trade is control: there are no presets, no timer and no slow cook. A one-switch cooker is dependable for white rice and less forgiving for brown.

It is a fine second cooker for gatherings, or a primary one for someone who only eats white rice. Skip it if you want unattended grain variety.
products.idealFor: Parties and families who eat mostly white rice.
products.skipIf: You cook brown rice or grains often.

products.name: AROMA Rice Cooker, 3-Cup (Uncooked) / 6-Cup (Cooked), Small Rice Cooker, Oatmeal Cooker, Soup Maker
products.verdict: A 1.5-quart cooker with a PFAS-free ceramic pot, built for one to three people.
products.description:
This small Aroma turns 3 cups of raw rice into 6 cooked, in a 1.5-quart pot coated with CoreCoat ceramic that the maker describes as naturally nonstick and PFAS-free. It is one-touch, switches automatically to keep warm, has measuring lines in the pot, and can also do oatmeal, soup and dips. The body is about 8.1 by 8 by 8.9 inches.

It lands fifth because a coating that avoids PFAS is a genuine reason to choose it, which the larger BLACK+DECKER cannot claim, but it has no presets or timer. Small batches also mean it will not feed a crowd. It outranks the other plain Aroma because of the ceramic pot.

It suits singles, couples and anyone who wants to avoid traditional nonstick. A manufacturer coating claim is not proof of long-term durability, so treat the ceramic with a wooden spoon.
products.idealFor: Singles and couples avoiding traditional nonstick.
products.skipIf: You cook for four or more.

products.name: BLACK+DECKER Rice Cooker 6-Cup (Cooked) with Steaming Basket, Removable Non-Stick Bowl, White
products.verdict: A 300W, ETL-listed starter with a steam vent that keeps moisture off the cabinets.
products.description:
This model cooks 1 to 6 cups using a 3/4 cup measuring cup, and it ships with a steaming basket, rice cup and spoon. The nonstick bowl is removable and dishwasher safe, a steam vent aims moisture away from overhead cabinets, and the unit is ETL listed at 120V and 300W. It stands about 9 by 5.5 by 10 inches.

Sixth place follows from how little it does beyond the basics. The manual offers rice-to-water ratios, and the listing notes that adding water changes texture, which is a candid way of saying you will tune it by hand. It is lighter on wattage than the Cosori, and slower.

Buy it for a dorm or small kitchen. For anything beyond white rice, step up.
products.skipIf: You want grain presets or a timer.

products.name: Aroma Housewares ARC-363-1NGB 3 Uncooked/6 Cups Cooked Rice Cooker, Steamer, Multicooker, Black
products.verdict: One-touch cooking with a steam tray, so a side dish cooks above the rice.
products.description:
The ARC-363 cooks 2 to 6 cups of rice with one-touch operation and an automatic warm cycle. A steam tray lets you cook vegetables or fish while rice cooks below, the nonstick inner pot is dishwasher safe, and the maker describes it as BPA free. The body measures about 8.1 by 9.5 by 9.4 inches.

It places seventh because it is nearly the same as the cheaper small cookers but without the ceramic pot or the oatmeal and soup features the other Aroma advertises. The simultaneous steaming is its distinguishing feature.

Choose it for a small household that likes steaming. It is a competent unit that does not stand out.
products.idealFor: Small households who steam vegetables with rice.
products.skipIf: You want a ceramic pot or digital control.

products.name: Elite Gourmet ERC-003X Rice Cooker, Keep Warm, White, 6 Cups Cooked | 3 Cups Uncooked
products.verdict: A tempered-glass lid, cool-touch handles and a keep-warm switch for under $30.
products.description:
The ERC-003X cooks up to 3 cups of uncooked rice, 6 cups cooked, then flips to keep warm. The inner pot lifts out so you can serve at the table, the lid is tempered glass, the side handles stay cool, and a measuring cup and spatula come with it. It also makes soups and stews, according to the maker.

It ranks last because it offers the least: no steam tray is listed, no coating details, no presets. It is cheap and does the one thing it promises.

It is the right first cooker for a student or a gift. If you can stretch to the Aroma pot-style models, you gain a better pot.
products.skipIf: You want steaming or any presets.

methodology.title: Cooking control
methodology.description: Fuzzy logic, sensor-based temperature control and presets for brown rice and grains rate higher than a single on/off heating cycle.

methodology.title: Capacity and fit
methodology.description: We compare stated uncooked and cooked capacities with household size, and footprint with typical counter space.

methodology.title: Keep-warm and timers
methodology.description: Automatic warm cycles, delay timers and the length of keep-warm decide how well a cooker fits a working day.

methodology.title: Pot and cleanup
methodology.description: Coating type, dishwasher-safe parts and removable lids affect daily use and long-term wear.

methodology.title: Extras and value
methodology.description: Steam trays, slow cook modes and accessories are weighed against where each cooker sits inside the $100 limit.

whatMatters.detail: A basic cooker heats until the water boils off, then clicks to warm. Sensor or fuzzy logic cookers watch temperature and adjust the cycle, which helps with brown rice, small batches and sticky varieties. Look for the words sensor, fuzzy logic or multiple rice presets in the listing, and expect to pay more for them.

whatMatters.factor: The cup that comes in the box
whatMatters.detail: A rice cooker cup is usually about three quarters of a standard cup, so 3 cups of rice from the box scoop equals less than 3 kitchen cups. Always use the supplied cup with the lines in the pot, or your ratios will be wrong. Check the listing for the phrase use only the included measuring cup.

Cooked capacity is roughly double the uncooked figure, and the uncooked number is the one that matters. A 3-cup uncooked cooker feeds about three people, while a 10-cup model suits a large family. Choose a size close to your usual batch, as a half-empty large pot cooks less evenly.

Traditional nonstick, ceramic and uncoated pots all behave differently over time. Ceramic coatings such as CoreCoat avoid PFAS, while nonstick coatings scratch if you use metal tools. Check which coating is named and use a plastic or wooden spatula whichever you choose.

Keep warm holds rice at serving temperature, and a delay timer starts the cook while you are out. Basic cookers hold warm for hours but can dry the bottom layer, so a timer that finishes just before dinner is better. Look for stated hours of keep warm and for a delay function.

howToChoose.intro: Cooker size should match your usual batch, since both too small and too large give worse rice.

cards.label: Digital
cards.text: Offers presets for brown rice, steam and flash rice, plus Sensor Logic or fuzzy logic on the Aroma digital models and the Cosori. Worth it if you cook varied grains or want a timer.

cards.label: One-touch
cards.text: Cooks rice and clicks to warm, as on the BLACK+DECKER and the small Aroma models. Simple, cheap and dependable for white rice, but less forgiving with brown rice.

howToChoose.note: Choose digital if you cook rice more than twice a week.

rows: Soup and oatmeal in a small pot

howToChoose.subheading: For Brown Rice and Grains Specifically

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A dedicated brown rice or grain preset, a longer cook cycle and a delay timer, since brown rice needs more water and time than white.

cards.label: In this ranking
cards.text: The Cosori offers three grain programmes and texture options, and the Aroma digital models have a brown rice preset. The one-touch models are not designed for it.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You want induction heating, pressure cooking or a Japanese-style inner pot, which lie above $100. Inside this budget, the Cosori is the upper end, and paying near $100 gets you the best programme depth.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You eat mostly white rice. A cooker under $30 does that well, and the Aroma digital at $30 to $50 adds presets for almost no extra money.

faq.q: Can these cookers make rice for sushi or risotto?
faq.a: They cook sushi-style short-grain rice well when you rinse it first and use the pot's water lines. Risotto needs stirring, so a rice cooker is the wrong tool, though the Cosori's saute function helps start a pilaf.

faq.q: What is the most common rice cooker mistake?
faq.a: Using a regular kitchen cup. Cooker cups are smaller, so use the supplied cup and the water lines in the pot, as the Aroma listing itself warns.

faq.q: Is the Cosori worth more than an Aroma digital?
faq.a: If you cook varied grains, yes. It adds fuzzy logic, 18 programmes and a 24-hour delay timer. For white rice and simple steaming, the Aroma digital at $30 to $50 does the job.

faq.q: How do I set it up for the first time?
faq.a: Wash the inner pot and accessories, rinse the rice until the water runs mostly clear, add water to the line for your rice type and press cook. Follow the manual's ratios for brown rice.

faq.q: How do I clean and care for the pot?
faq.a: Remove the inner pot and wash it with a soft sponge, or put it in the dishwasher if the listing allows. Wipe the heating plate and steam vent dry, and use a plastic spoon to protect the coating.

faq.q: Can I leave rice on keep warm overnight?
faq.a: A few hours is fine for most cookers, and the Cosori lists 24 hours. For food safety refrigerate leftovers within a few hours rather than leaving rice warm for a day.

finalTake: The Cosori 10-cup is the best rice cooker under $100 for people who cook rice often, because fuzzy logic, texture programmes and a delay timer change the result. The Aroma digital 4-cup is the better value for most families, and the Aroma 20-cup is the pick for a crowd. If you only need white rice, the Elite Gourmet and BLACK+DECKER models cost under $30 and do exactly that.
